detail.longDescription: Open almost any app today and you will see an AI button waiting for you. Email has it. Spreadsheets have it. Note-taking apps, photo editors, code editors, and even the plain text box. The message is the same everywhere: "Ask AI." Some of these features are useful. But a growing number seem to have been added for a different reason: because every product is expected to include AI, not because people actually asked for it. That is a mistake. It can hurt the people using these tools, and it can also damage trust in AI itself. The two-second problem Here is a simple example. You spot a typo in a sentence. You can fix it in two seconds: click, delete a letter, type the correct one, and move on. Now look at the AI route. You open the assistant panel, think about how to phrase the request, type something like, "fix the spelling mistake in the second paragraph," wait for the reply, read it to make sure it did not change anything else, and then decide whether to accept it. Even if the AI is fast and correct, you still spent more time, more attention, and more mental energy than the task deserved. This is the heart of the problem. A tool that takes longer than doing the task yourself is not a help. It is a detour. People are not irrational about this. We are always measuring how much effort a task costs, even when we do not notice it. If asking the tool is harder than doing the task ourselves, we stop using it. It does not matter how impressive the technology is. Humans are built to do things, not describe them For most of human history, our tools have been physical and direct. We pick up a hammer and hit the nail. We turn the steering wheel and the car turns. Good interfaces over the last few decades, from the mouse to the touchscreen, worked because they kept that direct link: you act, and the result appears right away. Prompting breaks that link. Instead of doing the thing, you have to describe it in words to a system that is trying to understand you, then check whether it got it right. For big, messy, creative, or research-heavy tasks, that tradeoff can be worth it. For small, simple, familiar tasks, it is a step backward. Our habits are built around skill and speed. When we are good at something, we want to use that skill. A designer who can move a shape into place does not want to type, "move the logo a little to the left." A developer who knows the shortcut does not want to explain a rename in a chat box. The novelty curve At first, people try every AI feature. It is new, and curiosity is strong. But novelty fades. After a few weeks, people settle into what is actually faster for them, and the rest gets ignored. This pattern is familiar. Voice assistants were supposed to replace screens, yet most people use them for timers and music. Many features that launched with big excitement quietly became things nobody clicks. If AI is bolted onto everything, a large share of those features will follow the same path. And that leads to the real danger. How this hurts the technology itself It creates AI fatigue. When every product keeps shouting, "powered by AI," the label stops meaning much. People learn to tune it out, even in the places where AI is genuinely useful. It damages trust. Every time an AI feature gets in the way, gives the wrong answer on a simple task, or changes something you did not want changed, trust drops. People do not separate one AI feature from AI in general. One bad experience colors the next one. It hides the real strengths. AI is good at summarizing long content, drafting from scratch, searching through huge amounts of information, explaining unfamiliar topics, and handling repetitive work at scale. When it is spread too thinly across every button, those strengths get buried under gimmicks. It pushes teams to build for demos, not for users. When the goal is to ship "an AI feature," the question becomes, "where can we add AI?" instead of, "what problem are people actually trying to solve?" Products get cluttered, and the things that matter most get less attention. How this hurts people It adds friction to tasks that were already easy. Menus get heavier, interfaces get noisier, and simple actions now compete with suggestions, pop-ups, and assistants. It can weaken skills. If people hand over every small task, from writing a sentence to doing a quick calculation, the habit of doing those things themselves fades. Not every skill needs to be preserved, but the ability to think clearly is worth protecting. It takes away choice. When AI is the default and the old way is hidden or removed, users are no longer choosing. They are being steered. It creates a new job: checking. Every AI result needs review. For a big task, that review is often worth it. For a tiny task, it can cost more than the task itself. The long-term risk: people go back to trusting themselves This is the part that tech companies should worry about most. If AI keeps showing up in places where it is not needed, people will not just ignore it. They will start to believe that AI is more trouble than it is worth. And once that belief takes hold, it becomes much harder to change, even for the situations where AI really does help. Humans have a strong preference for their own judgment when the stakes are low and their skill is high. That is not a flaw. It is common sense. A technology that wants lasting adoption has to respect that instinct. What good AI integration looks like This is not an argument against AI. It is an argument for using it where it earns its place. A useful test is this: Is it faster than doing it by hand? If not, it should not be the default option. Is the task heavy, repetitive, or hard to start? AI is strongest here. Can the user skip it easily? The manual option should stay simple and visible. Does it stay out of the way? Helpful suggestions that appear only when needed are better than constant prompts. Is the result easy to check? The cost of review should be low. The best AI features often barely feel like AI at all. They just remove a boring step, quietly, at the exact moment you need it. Conclusion The companies that win the next decade will not be the ones with the most AI buttons. They will be the ones that understand one basic truth about people: we reward tools that save us effort, and we ignore tools that add to it. If you can fix something with your own hand in a few seconds, you should not need to write a prompt to do it. Build AI for the moments when your own hands are not enough: the hard problems, the blank pages, the mountains of information. Do that well, and people will use it willingly. Force it into every corner, and they will learn to look away. # ai # productivity # learning # webdev # software # coding # development # engineering # inclusive # community When AI Gets Added to Everything, Nobody Wins
